children: Is Tesla
a buy, hold, or sell right now?
Seeking Alpha analysts
, and Daniel Jones weigh in.
Jack Bowman: Tesla
is a Hold for me because it's impossible to value due to the Elon premium or the (likely) possibility that it will merge with SpaceX

. But I think the news of winding down Cybertruck production in Texas is bullish for Tesla as it pivots to a market much more friendly to its brand and a better product, their autonomous cabs. They are much better off competing with Alphabet's
Waymo and Uber
than Ford
and Stellantis
in general.
(Jack Bowman runs the SA investing group ETF Portfolio Mechanics.)
Michael Del Monte: Sell rating. Tesla

has delayed volume production of Optimus by a year due to AI development and mechanical challenges. The company is investing heavily in expanding production of the Cybercab, which may become a successful business model over time, but may also be faced with mismatched timing between sunsetting consumer vehicle models and ramping up the robotaxi program.
Yiannis Zourmpanos: Tesla
is a Hold. FSD adoption is improving, but weak cash conversion, heavy capital requirements, and an elevated valuation limit upside despite the recent sell-off.
Daniel Jones: In my professional opinion, Tesla

has got to be one of the most overvalued companies on the market right now. This was the sentiment that I expressed about the business when I last reaffirmed it as a Strong Sell candidate back in late October. Revenue ended up falling year-over-year for the third quarter. This came as vehicle deliveries and average selling prices declined. The company was seeing growth in some categories, such as with FSD subscriptions and services revenue. But those account for just a small portion of the overall corporate pie.

Management has been lucky to be put into a slightly better competitive position, as other players in the automotive market have pared back on their electric vehicle ambitions. Examples here include General Motors
and Ford

, both of which have booked billions of dollars over the last 12 months or so in charges. I was particularly surprised by General Motors, considering it had rapidly become the second largest player in the U.S. EV market. But I digress.

At the time, Tesla was trading at about 240.5 times earnings and 100.4 times operating cash flow. In previous articles, I had even projected out that robust financial performance matching even the rosiest assumptions management seemed to offer would translate to investors having to wait years for the business to become attractively priced.

Unfortunately, some of its more ambitious opportunities have also fallen short of expectations. For years, the company had been promising a significant ramp-up of its robotaxi business. But as I detailed in my article, the business continues to be dominated by Alphabet's
Waymo and its drastically larger market position.
Recently, Elon Musk announced Tesla

will even be winding down the Cybertruck production at its Gigafactory in Texas in the middle of next year to make way for Cybercab production. But with Waymo having a massive operational advantage over the business, I don’t see it being able to scale up to compete in the long run.

Some investors are certainly optimistic about the humanoid robot that the company is working on, known as Optimus. This has created a lot of optimism as a new market opportunity for the business. I pointed out the challenges that the company faced here, including the fact that even if they achieved the kind of traction they were targeting, the best-case scenario would be only around $20B in additional annual revenue. For a company that, at that time, had a market capitalization of $1.62T, that was little more than a rounding error. Naturally, I still have the firm rated a Strong Sell today.
(Daniel Jones runs the SA investing newsletter Crude Value Insights.)
